title: EPA testing for lead contamination after lead azide detonation in Iowa
summary: The Army detonated the country's stockpile of lead azide. Now EPA teams are testing the soil, air and water for any lead contamination.

Now EPA teams are testing the soil, air and water for any lead contamination. Sponsor Message Transcript A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in eastern Iowa for lead contamination. The Army detonated thousands of pounds of lead azide on Wednesday. That's the stuff bombs are made with. The Army said it was unstable and a controlled explosion would've been the only way to get rid of it. Iowa Public Radio's Eliza Billingham is now with us. So, Eliza, let's start with the explosion itself and why the Army is calling it a success. ELIZA BILLINGHAM, BYLINE: Of course. The detonation took place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, and the major concern around this detonation was how much lead would be released in the air when this lead azide exploded. The Army worked to mitigate the explosion. The barrels were already underground, and then those bunkers were covered with tarps, water, and particle-collecting foam. And the EPA has been running tests ever since the explosion, and so far, it has not found any lead in the air. Shortly after the detonation, Major General Eric Shirley said the results exceeded his expectations. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) ERIC SHIRLEY: Every indication is that all of the munitions that were employed absolutely reduced the lead azide threat. MARTÍNEZ: All right. So tell us about the testing that's going on. How's it happening? BILLINGHAM: The EPA says it has about 300 people sampling the air, ground and nearby surface water for lead contamination. Lead is dangerous because it's a neurotoxin. It's especially dangerous to children and people who are pregnant because of how it can inhibit childhood development. The EPA has set legal limits for how much lead can be on windowsills and floors of houses, for example, so it and the Army are watching for lead levels on surfaces near the detonation zone to see if they exceed those limits, but so far, the EPA says its measurements haven't shown any lead dust. MARTÍNEZ: Now, what's been the reaction from residents? Because - I don't know - I'd be worried if I were there. BILLINGHAM: Right. The reaction has been mixed. The Army told some residents who lived within 5 miles of the detonation that it might be best to evacuate. And some people in that radius did leave their houses, but not everyone. Alan Kleinkopf lives in a house right around the corner from the plant's headquarters. He and his wife did leave their house yesterday morning but came back around noon, and he saw his home didn't seem to have any damage, and Kleinkopf said that made him feel pretty good. ALAN KLEINKOPF: I think the U.S. government has done the best that they could with their mitigating efforts that they put into place. BILLINGHAM: But after this past week and a half of delays and mixed messaging about the detonation, other residents have lost trust in the Army, and they're hesitant to trust the EPA's initial readings. They want independent monitoring. And the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois are sampling around the region, so we should know in a few days if their measurements line up with the EPA's. MARTÍNEZ: I wish them luck on that. Now, Iowa's governor, Kim Reynolds, she declared a disaster emergency for the three counties in southeastern Iowa. So what does a disaster emergency do for the people who actually live there? BILLINGHAM: That opens up the path to FEMA funding, and FEMA says it's ready to assist anyone who thinks they need relief. The public library in Burlington, which is right next to Middletown, said it has service navigators every week who help people navigate state and federal aid, so those people will be a great resource for anyone looking for FEMA funding. And the Army claims office is also in touch with residents in case anyone wants to file personal injury or property damage claims with the Army. MARTÍNEZ: All right. That's Eliza Billingham of Iowa Public Radio. Thanks a lot, Eliza. BILLINGHAM: Happy Thanksgiving. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved.
